name: unit-model-compare
notes:
Flip 'load-shedding model' live: loss vs node.js, identical sine load (period 200s) and identical knobs otherwise. Loss settles clean, ~1.5% errors, error line flat near zero after the initial transient. node.js: peak instances jumps from 6 to 9, errors rise to ~30% and stay elevated for the rest of the run, not just during the transient.

Two things are true at once here, both worth saying out loud:

1. The controller isn't blind. cpuReport (standing in for event-loop utilization) does rise with real load and does trigger scale-out, unlike an earlier version of this demo where the reported metric was wired to raw inFlight/concurrency and barely moved. But ELU saturates at 100% and stays pinned there whether you're 10% over capacity or 10x over -- it's a real signal, just a magnitude-blind, already-late one. That's why it reacts (unlike a metric that's actually hidden) but still ends up worse than loss.

2. The sustained (not just transient) elevated error rate has a second, distinct cause: Instance.terminate() marks every in-flight request on a killed instance as 'error'. Loss-model instances cap concurrency at the configured slot count (default 16), so a scale-in kills at most 16 requests. The node.js model has no such cap -- under sustained sine load it can be carrying hundreds of in-flight requests per instance. Every scale-in cycle the sine forces (instances tracking the wave, same as loss does) destroys far more in-flight work on the node.js side. Unbounded-concurrency units are dangerous to scale in, not just dangerous to scale up under.
